question: After long exercise, cyclists ate carbohydrate either at once or two hours later. How did their muscle glycogen compare after 24 hours?
options: Much higher if eaten at once
Higher if eaten two hours later
answer: About the same either way. Ivy's 1988 study had shown glycogen refills fastest right after exercise, and that a two-hour delay slows the early rate. But Parkin and colleagues found no difference at 8 or 24 hours once enough carbohydrate was eaten. The rush matters when the next session is hours away, not a day.
move: Ask over what stretch of time a head start still counts.
trap: Stretching the fast early refilling into an advantage for the whole day.
source: Parkin et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 1997
reference: Parkin, Carey, Martin, Stojanovska & Febbraio, Muscle glycogen storage following prolonged exercise: effect of timing of ingestion of high glycemic index food, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 1997
